title: Guru Ram Das close
hookLine: a routine, a city, and songs of longing: the fourth Guru's way

lines: AN ALARM, A HORSE, A FACE.
cards: An alarm clock in the dark. A horse dressed for a wedding. A face you ache to see.
A pool with a market at its edge. A man kneeling at a visitor's feet. Lay those on a table and they look like five different stories.
They're all one Guru: Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, Mahala four. Today his section closes with one question: what holds those pieces together?

teach.h: A ROUTINE: A DAY WITH A SHAPE.
teach.b: Three strands run through his days on this path. The first is a routine.

His salok on the Gursikh gave a clock, not a definition: rise early, make the effort, bathe, remember the Name; then, sitting and standing, with breath and mouthful, keep remembering; then help someone else remember, and the Guru asks for your dust.
A day with a shape. The second strand is a city.

teach.h: A CITY: THE ROUTINE AMONG OTHERS.
teach.b: Tradition says he set a pool, a bazaar and a sangat side by side in Ramdaspur: the routine given a place to live, among other people, in the middle of buying and selling. The third strand is longing.
The Ghorian, the horse songs, with the body as a gift that carries the soul home. The hymn of separation in Sri Rag: the ache, the friends you ask, the sight that heals it.
And in the stories, the humility of a Guru who kneels. Here's how they fit. A routine without longing can harden into a chore, boxes ticked.
Longing without a routine can drift, a beautiful ache that never gets out of bed. And both of them, without a city, stay private. Guru Ram Das holds all three together.
The longing gives the routine its warmth.
The routine gives the longing somewhere to go each morning.

And the city, and the kneeling, keep both turned toward other people. Sikh tradition says he passed the Guruship to his son Arjan, who carries the Name into a new set of hymns. That's where the path goes next.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Ram Das in the morning and evening prayers that include his hymns, at his gurpurab, and at the Harmandir Sahib in the city tradition says he began.

games.q: what does “guru ram das close” mean?
o: the hymn Guru Ram Das sang to close each day
a routine, a city and longing, held by a Guru who kneels
the closing of the bazaar he built at Ramdaspur

games.q: the fourth Guru's days: tap the pairs.
p: a routine: a day with a shape
a pool, a bazaar, a sangat
the body, a horse ridden home

s: Guru Ram Das's teaching on this path is only about rules for the morning
it's a routine, a city and songs of longing, held together.
Sikh tradition says Guru Ram Das passed the Guruship to his son Arjan
Arjan becomes the next Guru, and his hymns come next.

games.q: you have a good morning routine, but it's starting to feel like boxes to tick. which strand of Guru Ram Das's way would warm it?
o: longing: the ache for the Beloved's sight.
games.why: in his hymns, longing is what gives the routine its warmth, and the routine gives longing somewhere to go.

practice: Look back at the mornings since this stretch began, without grading them: did you rise a little earlier, even once, and what met you first?
Then choose what tomorrow's first minutes will hold, and add one thing from these days, a breath for someone you miss, or thanks for the horse you ride. If you pray, Waheguru can open the morning.

wordCard.voice: Guru Ram Das close. A routine, a city, and songs of longing, held together by a Guru who kneels. Today's word.

orig.note: Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, whose hymns carry the heading Mahala four.

carryVoice: Your line: the fourth guru's way. Longing gives the routine its warmth, and the routine gives longing a road. Until tomorrow.
